Open Mercato 

 Open Mercato Core is MIT licensed 

 Open Mercato - the AI-Engineering Foundation Framework. Start with 80% done. 

Open Mercato is an open-source TypeScript framework on Next.js and PostgreSQL. It ships ready business modules for CRM, ERP, commerce and more, so a new app starts as a working back office. It is built for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor get the rules and skills that say where code goes, and Cezar, the agentic development IDE, runs each task in its own git worktree and streams it live. It is for teams and developers building business apps and backends, and for business owners who want one.

 

 No terminal? Open Mercato Cloud gives you the same app in the browser, with Claude Code, Codex and Cezar already inside (account required).

 Prefer to delegate? Paste this line into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor:

 

 [!NOTE]
 For AI coding agents. To build an app, scaffold it with npx create-mercato-app --preset --agents all --init-git (or a comma-separated list of claude-code , codex , cursor , github-copilot ) and never clone this repository unless the human wants to change Open Mercato Core. If the request is ambiguous, such as "install this repo", ask that one question first. After scaffolding, the app's own AGENTS.md takes over and every task starts with om-help . Work one stage at a time: ask the You decide question and offer the bold default, do Run , confirm every Done when box. Stop at every "You decide" and at the spec's Open Questions.

 Quick start · Cloud · Cezar · Modules · Docs · Tutorials and videos · Discord · Contributing 

 
 Kaldi & Co. is a fictional specialty coffee roaster in Lisbon. The screens on this page are from the app built with the four stages below, with the roaster's own demo data loaded through the API. 

 What is Open Mercato

AI code assistants generate code. They do not decide where it goes, how it is layered, or whether it stays consistent across 30 or 50 engineers in a team. Open Mercato gives them a foundation that does:

- Architecture-aware AI harness. Every app ships an AGENTS.md and skills that tell the agent where code, modules, data models and UI belong, how to troubleshoot and how to upgrade, from a data table or a design-system form up to a whole feature with unit and integration tests. The open-mercato/skills collection adds code review, ticketing and debugging.
- Spec-first. Specs live next to the code in .ai/specs/ and drive the agent's work: plan, approve, then implement.
- Start with 80% done. Dozens of business modules already work together: customers, catalog, sales, warehouse, portal, workflows and more (what's in the box).
- Unattended when you want it. Cezar runs the same skills in parallel, on a schedule or on GitHub events, and never merges on its own.
- No lock-in. You own the code. The core is MIT with no per-seat licence; enterprise modules are licensed separately.

Built for CTOs and team leads who already rolled out Cursor or Copilot and noticed it is not enough, and for developers who want to build professional business apps and backends without constantly checking their back.

 Get started

Pick your row. Everyone who builds an app goes through the same four stages, and each stage has the same shape: You decide (a question with a bold default), Run (commands or the exact prompt), Done when (checks you can tick), then a screenshot from the Kaldi run. The whole run, from npx to a working module with a business rule and a cafe login, took one agent evening: about 2 hours 10 minutes of wall time, the long parts being the first install and the module build.

 A developer Minute 10 in your terminal Hour 1, Day 1, Month 1 
 An AI coding agent the note at the top of this page every stage in order, stopping at each You decide 
 A module author Build and publish a module create-mercato-module, then list it in Open Mercato Modules 
 A core contributor Change Open Mercato Core CONTRIBUTING.md 

 No terminal: Open Mercato Cloud

Open Mercato Cloud is a hosted trial workspace (Beta) with the app already initialised. Inside you get:

- the templates crm , classic or empty , demo users, a View as role switcher and a live preview;
- VS Code in the browser and a web terminal;
- Claude Code and Codex, on managed credits by default or on your own subscription ( claude auth login --claudeai , codex login --device-auth );
- Cezar , preinstalled as the AI Coding Agent tab (Beta): the default way to drive the agent here;
- PostgreSQL and Redis. There is no Docker inside, and it is not production hosting.

Keep your work: run gh auth login in the web terminal, then use Create repository and Create PR in the portal, or Export sandbox (a tar with your workspace and a database dump). If sign-up says "Email registration is currently closed", you are on the waitlist. No terminal: Open Mercato Cloud

Open Mercato Cloud is a hosted trial workspace (Beta) with the app already initialised. Inside you get:

  • the templates crm, classic or empty, demo users, a View as role switcher and a live preview;
  • VS Code in the browser and a web terminal;
  • Claude Code and Codex, on managed credits by default or on your own subscription (claude auth login --claudeai, codex login --device-auth);
  • Cezar, preinstalled as the AI Coding Agent tab (Beta): the default way to drive the agent here;
  • PostgreSQL and Redis. There is no Docker inside, and it is not production hosting.

Keep your work: run gh auth login in the web terminal, then use Create repository and Create PR in the portal, or Export sandbox (a tar with your workspace and a database dump). If sign-up says "Email registration is currently closed", you are on the waitlist. Watch the Open Mercato Cloud tour, or follow the video course for non-developers built on the sandbox (Polish only).

Minute 10: a running back office

You decide: which starter? classic (CRM, catalog, sales, warehouse, portal, demo data) · crm · wms · empty. Which agents? all (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, which gets instructions only, no hooks) · one of them.

Run in a terminal, as is. You need Docker running (Docker Desktop, OrbStack or Colima) and about 8 GB of free RAM; mise installs Node.js 24 and Yarn 4 for you. On Windows use WSL2 and see Developing on Windows. All options: installation guides.

curl https://mise.run | sh && export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$HOME/.local/share/mise/shims:$PATH"
mise use -g node@24 yarn@4      # Node.js 24 and Yarn 4; skip both lines if you already have them
npx create-mercato-app my-app --preset classic --agents all --init-git
cd my-app
yarn setup

yarn setup creates missing environment files, installs dependencies, picks the services, applies migrations, initializes demo data when needed, and starts the dev runtime. Without a service flag it reuses the PostgreSQL, Redis and Meilisearch configured in .env when they answer and their credentials verify; when nothing answers it starts this app's Docker Compose services on the configured ports; when those ports belong to something else (another checkout's containers, a database with different credentials) it starts an isolated Compose stack on free ports and says why. Interactive terminals show the choice with that pick as the default; the flags select a mode explicitly: --infra (Compose on configured ports), --random-ports (isolated Compose stack on free ports), --ephemeral (disposable Testcontainers services for the session) and --no-infra / --reuse-services (the services in .env, no Docker calls). Isolated options synchronize the service ports and URLs; ephemeral settings are restored when the session exits. Re-running reuses existing infrastructure and keeps your data. Before database setup, connections and credentials are verified with a PostgreSQL query, Redis PINGs and the protected Meilisearch API. Remote database migrations and initialization additionally require an exact-target acknowledgement such as --allow-remote-database=staging.example:5432/app_db; local reuse remains automatic. Setup failures print the manual install, initialization and dev commands.

Without Docker

Docker only runs the services for you. Without it, run them yourself; only PostgreSQL is required:

Service Needed for Install, for example
PostgreSQL 15+ everything sudo apt install postgresql · brew install postgresql@17 · Windows installer
Redis 7 optional: cache, queues and events shared across processes sudo apt install redis-server · brew install redis
Meilisearch 1.11 optional: full-text search curl -L https://install.meilisearch.com | sh
  1. Create the database with a user that may create extensions on the first run (unaccent and pg_trgm, which ship with PostgreSQL; add pgvector only for vector search). With the defaults from .env.example: sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER USER postgres PASSWORD 'postgres'" and sudo -u postgres createdb open-mercato (on macOS with Homebrew: createuser -s postgres, then createdb -U postgres open-mercato).
  2. If your user, password, host or port differ, set DATABASE_URL in .env; for the optional services, uncomment and set REDIS_URL, MEILISEARCH_HOST and MEILISEARCH_API_KEY.
  3. Run yarn setup. When Docker is missing but the database in .env answers, setup uses your services; yarn setup --no-infra forces that and makes no Docker calls at all.

A plain npx create-mercato-app my-app asks these questions plus Git init (its agent default is Claude Code). Without a terminal it silently picks classic, claude-code and no git, so agents always pass the flags and run yarn setup in the background; it picks services without prompting. If Docker is unavailable, follow Without Docker, or offer Open Mercato Cloud. To keep mise after this terminal closes, add eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate zsh)" (or bash) to your shell profile. Pushing to GitHub is optional and comes later, in Day 1.

In the Cloud: sign in or request access (registration may be closed, see the waitlist note), create a sandbox from the classic template, wait until it shows Running, then click Open app.

Done when

  • the terminal prints Backend URL http://localhost:3000/backend; the logins are admin@acme.com / secret, also superadmin@acme.com and employee@acme.com with the same password (the full box is in .mercato/logs/*-dev-setup-runner.log, or run yarn setup --verbose)
  • you open http://localhost:3000/backend and sign in as admin@acme.com / secret (Cloud: Open app, then View as Admin). Open it as localhost, not 127.0.0.1 or the machine's IP: the dev server serves its scripts to localhost only, so other hosts get a page that never finishes loading (on a remote box, use an SSH tunnel)
  • for agents: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' localhost:3000/login prints 200 and .agents/skills/om-help exists (if not, run yarn install-skills)
  • Customers lists demo companies and people, and Sales lists demo orders

In the Kaldi run this stage took about 11 minutes from npx to a working login (about 7 minutes of that was installing dependencies and the first setup, on an 8-core Linux box with warm caches). Stuck? See troubleshooting.
